lesson.subtitle: Lesson 1 -- The Clause That Broke
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Inês (Mock TBL) | Lesson 1 -- The Clause That Broke

paras: In cross-border deals, the clause that causes the most litigation is rarely the one the parties argued about. It is the earn-out: the part of the price that the seller only receives if the business hits certain targets after closing. On paper it looks like a fair compromise. In practice it hands the buyer control of the very numbers that determine what the seller gets paid.

A common pattern goes like this. The seller accepts a lower headline price in exchange for an earn-out worth thirty per cent of the total. The buyer, now running the company, decides to invest heavily in a new market. The investment is defensible, even sensible, and it depresses profit for exactly the two years the earn-out is measured over. The seller receives nothing, and nothing improper has happened.

Experienced counsel therefore stop negotiating the number and start negotiating the definitions. What counts as profit. Who prepares the accounts. Whether the buyer owes any duty to operate the business so as to give the earn-out a fair chance. English courts have been reluctant to imply that duty where the contract is silent, which means silence is a choice with consequences.

The practical lesson is uncomfortable. In an earn-out, the party with less leverage should spend its remaining leverage not on price, but on the machinery that measures performance. Ask who holds the pen after closing. Whatever the answer, write it down.

gist.prompt: Which sentence best captures the argument?
choices: Earn-outs are unfair and should be avoided in cross-border deals.
In an earn-out, the definitions matter more than the number.
English courts usually protect sellers in earn-out disputes.

language.title: Extract the expressions. Match each to the move it makes at the table.
words: "I'd want to understand what sits behind that number."
"Let me push back on one thing."
"Where does that leave my client if..."
"I can live with the number if we fix the definition."
"Can we park that and come back to it?"
defs: conditional acceptance — yes, with a price
trades a concession for the thing you actually want
tests the downside scenario out loud

language.text: These are not vocabulary items to memorise: they are moves. Notice that none of them says no, and none of them says yes. At C1 the difficulty is rarely the words — it is holding a position in a second language while staying pleasant.

items: Task 1 — obligatory · 16 min

You act for the SELLER of a logistics company. The buyer (your teacher, as Mr Hall) has proposed: lower headline price, plus an earn-out worth 30% measured on EBITDA over two years, accounts prepared by the buyer, no operating covenants.
The outcome you must produce

By the end, you and Mr Hall must have agreed OUT LOUD on three things: (1) who prepares the accounts, (2) one definition you have changed and how, and (3) what happens if the buyer opens a new market. Write nothing until you have all three.
The constraint
You may not simply demand a higher price. If you go there, Mr Hall will accept — and remove the earn-out protections you actually need.

task1.label: Useful language
items: I'd want to understand what sits behind that number.
That's workable in principle, provided that...
Let me push back on one thing.
Where does that leave my client if...?
I can live with the number if we fix the definition.
Can we park that and come back to it?
Help me understand the rationale.
On that basis, yes.
Task 2 — contingent on time · 10 min
Different type, same theme. Mr Hall's client will not move on the accounts point. Your client calls you and asks, in one minute, whether to sign.
Your task
Give the advice. Not the analysis — the advice, with the reason compressed into one sentence, and the risk named.

task2.text: Independent of Task 1: whatever happened in the negotiation, the client still has to decide. If time is short, this is the task that gets cut — never the Focus on Form.

form.title: Focus on Form — deferred correction
items: Your teacher noted errors during BOTH tasks without interrupting. Now they come back: two forms to reshape, two things that worked.
Which of the six expressions did you actually use? Which one did you reach for and not find?
Was there a moment when you said yes because the English ran out, not because you agreed?

wrapup.title: Wrap-up
items: In one sentence: what does a seller trade, and what should they buy with it?
Which expression will you use in a real call this month?
